A trading town on the Spree that became the capital of Prussia and, in 1871, of Germany. Binchun saw it in 1866; Min Yeong-hwan passed through on his way to the coronation in Moscow in 1896.
Roman Burdigala, a wine port on the Garonne that was English for three centuries. Rabban Sauma met the English king Edward I here in 1287.
France's naval port on the Mediterranean. Bonaparte's fleet for Egypt sailed from here in 1798, and an Ottoman envoy landed here on his way to Paris in 1720.
The port at the head of the Red Sea: Clysma to the Romans, al-Qulzum to the Arabs. Ships from India unloaded here for the overland road to the Nile, until the canal opened in 1869.
Built on a sandbar in 1859 for the northern mouth of the Suez Canal, and named for the khedive Said. Steamers to the East coaled here.
Rashid, a port on the western mouth of the Nile. French soldiers digging a fort here in 1799 found the stone that let Champollion read hieroglyphs.
Syene, Egypt's southern frontier at the first cataract, where the granite for obelisks was quarried. Eratosthenes measured the Earth from the noon sun here.
A harbour on the coast of Galilee, the last stronghold of the crusaders until 1291. The Polos took ship here in 1271; Bonaparte's siege failed before its walls in 1799.
Built by Herod Antipas on the Sea of Galilee and named for the emperor Tiberius. Its rabbis fixed the Hebrew Bible's vowels; the Mongols were beaten near here at ʿAyn Jālūt in 1260.
Laiazzo, the port of Cilician Armenia, where Venetian and Genoese ships met the caravans from Tabriz. The Polos landed here in 1271.
The island capital of the Itza Maya in Lake Petén Itzá, the last independent Maya kingdom. Spain took it only in 1697, and it became the town of Flores.
A trading town on the Laguna de Términos where Aztec merchants met the Maya and the Chontal canoe traders. Malinche was given to Cortés by the lords of this coast.
A port at the mouth of its river on the Gulf of Mexico, where by legend Quetzalcoatl sailed away east. Aztec merchants travelled here to trade with the Maya lands.
The first Spanish settlement in the Americas, built from the timbers of the wrecked Santa María on Christmas 1492. Columbus came back in 1493 to find it burned and its men dead.
One of the first Spanish towns on the South American mainland, by the pearl fisheries of Cubagua. Humboldt began his American travels here in 1799.
The northernmost Spanish town in New Spain when Cabeza de Vaca's party walked in from Texas in 1536. Coronado set out from here for the Seven Cities in 1540.
Cuba's first capital, founded by Velázquez in 1515. Cortés sailed from here for Mexico in 1518.
Can Pech, a Maya town on the Gulf coast, became the Spanish port of San Francisco de Campeche in 1540, walled against pirates.
The French port of Guiana, later the landing place for the penal colony. La Condamine came out of the Amazon here in 1744.
Founded in a mountain valley above the Caribbean in 1567, the birthplace of Bolívar. Che Guevara and Alberto Granado ended their journey here in 1952.
Chile's port, climbing its hills above the Pacific, the last great harbour before Cape Horn. The Beagle, the Challenger and Che Guevara all called here.
The first green valley south of the Atacama, on the Inca road to Chile. Almagro's army came down into it, starving, in 1536.
The capital of the Qolla kingdom near Lake Titicaca, taken by the Inca Pachacuti. It became an Inca provincial centre on the road to Kollasuyu.
A frontier fort of 1828 on the Pampas, which grew into a port. Darwin dug up giant fossil sloths at Punta Alta nearby in 1832.
A Jesuit mission on the plateau of Piratininga, the base of the bandeirantes who explored and raided the interior of Brazil.
A river port on the Amazon where Colombia, Peru and Brazil meet, beside Brazil's Tabatinga. Che Guevara left the Amazon here in 1952.
The capital of Madeira, settled by the Portuguese in the 1420s and rich on sugar. Columbus lived on the islands; Cook and Amundsen took on wine and water here.
A small river port in Andalusia whose sailors manned Columbus's ships. The three ships left here on 3 August 1492.
The capital of Mali in its golden age, from where Mansa Musa set out for Mecca in 1324. Its site is still argued over: Niani on the Sankarani is one candidate.
A salt-mining town in the middle of the Sahara whose houses and mosque were built of slabs of salt. Its salt was traded for gold in the Sudan; Ibn Battuta stayed ten days.
The Tuareg sultanate's town in the Aïr, whose mud minaret still stands. Askia Muhammad passed on his hajj in 1496, and Barth in 1850.
The capital of the Fezzan, where the caravan roads from Tripoli to Bornu met. Barth's expedition rested here in 1850.
The first Hormuz, on the mainland by the Minab river: Nearchus's fleet beached here in 325 BCE, and Marco Polo saw it in 1272. About 1300 its people moved to the island.
A desert city of wind towers and underground canals, the last home of the Zoroastrian faith in Iran. Marco Polo praised its silk cloth.
The frankincense port of Dhofar, now the ruins of al-Baleed by Salalah. Zheng He's fleet traded silk for incense here; Ibn Battuta found its people living on sardines.
A city at the head of the Indus delta where Alexander built a harbour and Nearchus's fleet was fitted out in 325 BCE. Its site has never been found.
The southern tip of India, a temple town where three seas meet. The Periplus called it Komarei, and Marco Polo, Comari.
Kollam, a pepper port of Kerala whose era began in 825. Arab merchants called it Kulam Mali; Polo, Coilum; the Ming, Xiao Gelan.
A harbour on the southern tip of Sri Lanka, the landfall for ships crossing from Arabia and China. Zheng He left a stone here in Chinese, Tamil and Persian in 1409.
The port of Bengal from which Buddhist pilgrims sailed home to China: Faxian in 411, Yijing in 685. Its harbour silted up, and the town is now Tamluk.
Bengal's seaport at the mouth of the Karnaphuli. Ibn Battuta landed here in 1346, and Zheng He's ships anchored here on their way to the Bengal court.
The first Muslim sultanate in Southeast Asia, on the north coast of Sumatra, which gave the island its name. Polo waited five months here for the monsoon; Ibn Battuta and Zheng He both called.
Kadaram, an old port of the Malay peninsula where ships waited for the wind to cross the Bay of Bengal. Yijing stopped here in 671, and the Chola fleet sacked it in 1025.
Malayu on the Batang Hari river, a Buddhist kingdom whose temple compound at Muaro Jambi was a seat of learning. Yijing stopped here in 671 on his way to India; Atisha came to study in 1012.
Prey Nokor, a Khmer river port that Vietnamese settlers made Gia Định in 1698. The French took it in 1859; Binchun's party passed in 1866.
The Korean border town on the Yalu, where every embassy to the Chinese court crossed the river. Pak Ji-won's party set out from here for Jehol in 1780.
A town on the road south from Beijing, where Marco Polo says the roads to Cathay and to Mangi part.
Isfijab, an old caravan town north of Tashkent. Changchun passed it on his way to Genghis Khan in 1221.
The capital of Kashmir on the Jhelum and its lakes, founded as Pravarapura in the 6th century. Xuanzang studied two years in the valley; Hyecho passed in the 720s.
The island capital of the Maldives, whose cowrie shells served as money from Bengal to West Africa. Ibn Battuta was its judge in 1343.
The Russian fort near the mouth of the Kamchatka river where Bering built his ship in 1728. The castaway Daikokuya Kōdayū wintered here.
The Arctic town of northern Norway, the starting point for sealers and polar expeditions. The Vega called here in 1878 on its way to the Northeast Passage.
An Iñupiat town at Point Barrow, the northern tip of Alaska, where whalers have lived for well over a thousand years. Rasmussen reached it in 1924.
An Inughuit settlement in Avanersuaq, northwest Greenland. Rasmussen's trading station of 1910 here was called Thule, the name archaeologists then gave the whole people.
The capital of Phrygia, King Midas's city. Alexander cut, or loosened, the famous knot on the wagon here in 333 BCE.
An oasis town deep in the Libyan desert, seat of the oracle of Amun. Alexander crossed the desert to consult it in 331 BCE.
Alexandria Eschate, Alexandria the Furthest, founded by Alexander on the Jaxartes in 329 BCE as the edge of his empire.
The Red Sea port of Mecca, made so by the caliph Uthman in 647. Pilgrims by sea land here; Ibn Battuta sailed from it.
Sinope, the Greek colony on the Black Sea's southern shore, home of Diogenes. Ibn Battuta sailed from here across the sea to the Crimea.
Bougie, the Hammadid capital on the Algerian coast, whose wax candles gave the French their word for candle. Fibonacci learned Arabic numerals here.
A copper town in the desert west of the Aïr, probably the ruins of Azelik. Ibn Battuta stayed here in 1353, and copper bars from its mines were traded as money.
The chief town of the oases of Tuat, a halt on the caravan road between Mali and the Mediterranean.
A desert city of southeast Iran, famous for its carpets and its turquoise. Marco Polo admired its embroidery and its falcons.
Polo's Camadi, a once-great market town of the Halil valley that he found in ruins, raided by the Karaunas. It is now Jiroft.
Polo's Cobinan, a town in the Kerman mountains where tutty, a zinc oxide for the eyes, was made.
Polo's Tonocain, a town of eastern Iran near the Dry Tree that marked the end of the world to him. It was renamed Ferdows in the 1930s.
Polo's Saba, where he was shown the tombs of the three Magi who had gone to Bethlehem.
Polo's Sapurgan, a town of the Afghan steppe whose melons, he wrote, were dried in strips and as sweet as honey.
Polo's Taican, a town below mountains of salt, he says, so large that the whole world could take from them until the end of time.
Polo's Pem, an oasis on the southern road round the Taklamakan, where jade was found in its river.
Charchan, one of the oasis kingdoms of the Han on the southern Silk Road, which Polo found wasted by Tatar raids.
The last oasis before the desert of Lop, where Polo's caravan rested a week before the month-long crossing.
Chaghan Nuur, the White Lake, where Kublai Khan had a palace and hunted cranes and swans on his way to and from Shangdu.
Polo's Cacanfu, a silk town on the canal country south of Beijing.
Polo's Cianglu, where, he says, salt was made from the earth and boiled; Changlu salt was famous through the Ming and Qing.
Polo's Cayu, a town on the Grand Canal beside its lake, north of Yangzhou.
Polo's Ghiuju, a town of Zhejiang on the road south to Fujian.
Polo's Quenlinfu, a town in the Fujian hills with three fine bridges, where he says sugar and silk were plentiful.
Polo's Caindu, in the mountains on the way to Yunnan, where he says salt was cut into cakes and used as money.
Polo's Cail, the pearl-fishing port of the Pandya kings on the Gulf of Mannar, where horses from Arabia were landed.
The town on the narrows between Euboea and the mainland, Venetian Negroponte from 1209 to 1470. The Polos sailed home past it.
Sebasteia, a town of central Anatolia on the caravan road east, which Polo calls Savast.
Polo's Arzinga, a town of Greater Armenia famous, he says, for its buckram cloth and its hot springs.
Theodosiopolis, a fortress city on the high plateau of eastern Anatolia guarding the road to Persia. Polo calls it Arziron.
The castle town of Date Masamune, who sent Hasekura Tsunenaga on an embassy to Spain and Rome in 1613 from the bay of Tsukinoura nearby.
A nitrate and copper port on the Atacama coast, Bolivian until the War of the Pacific made it Chilean in 1879.
A company town beside one of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world. Che Guevara visited the mine in 1952 and wrote about its miners; the town was emptied in 2007.
A frontier fort of 1881 in the lands of the Mapuche, the last to fall to Chile. Che's local newspaper interview made the two travellers 'leprosy experts'.
A town of southern Chile founded in 1739 as a frontier fort. Che and Alberto, their motorcycle failing, helped fight a fire here.
A town on Lake Nahuel Huapi in the Andes of Patagonia, settled by Swiss and German emigrants. The travellers crossed the lakes into Chile from here.
A seaside resort on the Atlantic south of Mar del Plata, where Che lingered with Chichina, the girl he would not see again.
A river port on the Ucayali where the road over the Andes reaches the Amazon. Che and Alberto took a boat downriver from here in 1952.
A leper colony on the Amazon in Peru where Che and Alberto worked for three weeks in 1952. On Che's birthday he swam across the river to the patients' side.
A port on a peninsula of the Persian Gulf, Rev-Ardashir under the Sasanians; Nearchus's Mesambria was probably here.
The merchants' harbour on the Sound, Denmark's capital, where ships into and out of the Baltic paid their toll.
A town of the Brabant cloth trade that became the seat of the Habsburg Netherlands and then of Belgium.
The baroque capital of Saxony on the Elbe, whose court made Europe's first true porcelain at Meissen nearby in 1710.
A city on the Oder, Bohemian, Habsburg, Prussian as Breslau and since 1945 Polish. The Mongols burned it in 1241.
Tolosa, the pink brick city of the Garonne, once the Visigoths' capital and the heart of the Cathar south.
A port in the marshes of the Lee in southern Ireland, grown from a monastery of St Finbarr.
Catherine the Great's port on the Black Sea, founded in 1794 to ship the grain of the steppe.

A fortress where the Oka meets the Volga, whose great summer fair drew the goods of Asia. Afanasy Nikitin waited here in 1466 to go down the Volga with an embassy to Shirvan, the first leg of his journey to India.
A Volga principality that rivalled Moscow for the lead of Russia in the 14th century. Afanasy Nikitin was a merchant of Tver.
The first Russian town in Siberia, founded in 1586 on the site of a Tatar town, on the road east from the Urals.
A Cossack fort of 1604 on the Tom, which became the learned city of Siberia.
'Ruler of the East', Russia's port on the Pacific, founded in 1860 on Haishenwai bay, ceded by the Qing that year.
The Pacific terminus of the Canadian Pacific Railway, named for George Vancouver, who charted these waters in 1792.
Joppa, the old port of Jerusalem, where pilgrims to the Holy Land came ashore for centuries.
An ancient city of the moon god Sin, where Abraham's family stopped and the Romans lost to Parthia at Carrhae in 53 BCE. The Mongols ruined it in 1271.
A frontier city between Rome and Persia, home of a famous school of Syriac learning. It is now Nusaybin.
Amida, a black basalt fortress city on the Tigris, besieged by Persia in 359 as Ammianus watched from its walls.
The shrine city of the Imam Reza, buried here in 818, and the great pilgrimage of Shi'a Iran.
A city below the Alborz at the edge of the land of the Assassins, and the Safavid capital from 1555.
The capital of Khwarazm on the lower Oxus, destroyed by Genghis Khan's sons in 1221 when they turned the river onto it. It was rebuilt, then left when the Oxus changed its course.
A Sogdian trading town on the Chu river, the westernmost fort of the Tang. Li Bai is said to have been born here; a Tang inscription found in 1982 confirmed its ruins at Ak-Beshim.
'Five Towns', the Tang's Beiting, then the summer capital of the Uyghurs of Turfan. Changchun stayed here in 1221.
The 'Stone Tower' in the Pamirs, the last town before the passes into Afghanistan, Xuanzang's Kebantuo.
Founded by Sultan Ahmad Shah in 1411 on the Sabarmati, the capital of Gujarat and a city of cotton weavers.
A Chola port on the Coromandel coast where the king of Srivijaya built a Buddhist monastery in 1006.
The capital Rajendra Chola built after his armies reached the Ganges; its great temple still stands. His fleet raided Srivijaya in 1025.
A great Buddhist monastery on the Ganges, where Atisha taught before he left for Tibet in 1040. It was destroyed about 1203.
The capital of the Garamantes in the Fezzan, desert people who dug underground canals and traded across the Sahara with Rome.
The capital of Bornu near Lake Chad, founded in 1814. Barth made it his base for five years of travel.
The capital of the sultanate of Damagaram, a caravan town between the Hausa cities and the Sahara.
A market town on Lake Tanganyika at the end of the ivory caravan road. Stanley found Livingstone here in 1871.
Kazeh, the trading town of the Nyamwezi country where the caravan roads from the coast to the lakes met.
The coast town where the ivory caravans from the interior ended, opposite Zanzibar. Livingstone's body was brought here in 1874.
A Portuguese trading post on the Zambezi, the furthest inland in Mozambique. Livingstone came down the river to it in 1856.
Guapondélig of the Cañari, then Tumebamba, the northern capital of the Inca where Huayna Capac was born. Spanish Cuenca was built on it in 1557.
Hatun Xauxa, an Inca centre in the Mantaro valley, which Pizarro briefly made the Spanish capital of Peru in 1534.

The tomb of the pharaoh Khufu, the tallest building on Earth for nearly four thousand years. Herodotus heard its story from priests two thousand years after it was raised, and it was already ancient to them.
A ring of great sarsens raised on Salisbury Plain, aligned with the midsummer sunrise. Its builders left no writing; by the Middle Ages it was said Merlin had flown the stones from Ireland.
Carved stone pillars raised by hunter-gatherers some seven thousand years before the pyramids, then deliberately buried. Its age was recognised only in 1994.
Ramesses II's temples cut into a Nubian cliff, facing the sunrise down the Nile. Sand buried them to the shoulders; Burckhardt glimpsed a colossal head above the dune in 1813.

Not one wall but many: for two thousand years dynasty after dynasty walled the northern frontier, each along its own line, while the walls of the last fell to ruin. The mark follows the wall of the age; the faint lines are the walls that went before.

phases.name: Warring States walls
phases.note: Rival states wall themselves off from one another and from the steppe: Qi in Shandong, Zhao, Yan and Qin in the north.

phases.name: Qin
phases.note: The First Emperor joins the northern walls into one, from Lintao to Liaodong.

phases.name: Han
phases.note: Han restores the Qin wall and carries it west along the Hexi Corridor to the Jade Gate, with beacons out toward Lop Nur, to guard the road to the West.

phases.name: Northern Qi and Sui
phases.note: Northern Qi raises a new line across Shanxi to the sea; Sui rebuilds it with forced labour.

phases.name: Tang
phases.note: With its frontier far out on the steppe, Tang builds no wall; the old ones crumble.

phases.name: Jin
phases.note: The Jurchen Jin dig border trenches behind ramparts far north across the Mongolian steppe; Genghis Khan's armies ride over them.

phases.name: Yuan
phases.note: Inside the Mongol empire the wall guards nothing and is left to ruin; only the pass at Juyongguan is adorned, with the Cloud Platform of 1345.

phases.name: Ming
phases.note: Ming rebuilds the wall from Shanhaiguan to Jiayuguan, faced in brick and stone after the 1570s: the wall seen today.

phases.name: Qing
phases.note: Once Qing armies pass Shanhaiguan in 1644 the wall is no longer a frontier, only a customs line and a slow ruin, until the twentieth century makes it a national symbol.

story: Some eight thousand clay soldiers buried to guard the First Emperor's tomb. Rebels burned the pits within a few years of his death, and they lay forgotten until farmers digging a well struck them in 1974.

The largest Buddhist monument in the world, a mountain of carved terraces in central Java. Deserted as the island's courts moved east, it vanished under ash and jungle until Raffles had it cleared in 1814.

A palace on a granite rock rising two hundred metres from the plain, with frescoed maidens painted on its face. The king who built it reigned only eighteen years; monks kept the rock for centuries after.
Buddhist halls cut into a river gorge, painted with the finest surviving murals of ancient India. Forgotten for a millennium, they were stumbled on by a British officer hunting a tiger in 1819.

Nearly a thousand stone figures carved from the crater of Rano Raraku and stood on platforms facing inland. When Roggeveen landed in 1722 many still stood; within a century and a half all had been pulled down.

Lines and figures scraped into the desert floor across hundreds of square kilometres: a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider. From the ground they are faint paths; they were first studied in 1927 and seen whole from the air.
Some five hundred painted cave temples cut into a cliff outside Dunhuang. In 1900 a monk found a sealed library of tens of thousands of manuscripts, among them the oldest dated printed book.
A sea-level canal from the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. Pharaohs and caliphs had cut canals from the Nile; this one, opened in 1869, cut the voyage from London to Bombay by nearly half.
Locks lift ships across the isthmus that Balboa crossed on foot in 1513. Its opening in 1914 ended the long passage around Cape Horn.
The Zambezi drops a hundred metres into a chasm a mile and a half wide. Its name here was Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders; Livingstone, shown it in 1855, named it for his queen.
A snow-capped volcano three degrees from the equator. When the missionary Rebmann reported snow on it in 1848, London geographers refused to believe him.
The Colorado River's gorge, a mile deep, home to the Havasupai. García López de Cárdenas reached the rim in 1540 and could find no way down.
A sandstone monolith in the centre of Australia, sacred to the Anangu for tens of thousands of years. William Gosse reached it in 1873 and named it Ayers Rock.
Japan's highest and most sacred mountain, a near-perfect volcanic cone last erupting in 1707. Pilgrims climbed it for centuries; Hokusai drew it thirty-six times.
The outflow of the Great Lakes pours over a broad ledge on its way to Lake Ontario. The friar Louis Hennepin, who saw it in 1678, gave Europe its first description.
Some 275 cascades along a horseshoe of the Iguazu, named for great water in Guarani. Cabeza de Vaca came upon it in 1541.
The deepest and oldest lake on Earth, holding a fifth of the world's fresh surface water. Russian Cossacks under Kurbat Ivanov reached its shore in 1643.
A salt lake at the lowest point on land, so dense a swimmer floats. It figures in Genesis, and Aristotle had heard that nothing could sink in it.
A pyramid of rock and snow in western Tibet, sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bon. Pilgrims walk around it rather than climb it; no one has stood on its summit.
A volcanic island in the Sunda Strait. Its eruption in 1883 was heard nearly five thousand kilometres away, and telegraph cables carried the news around the world within hours.
Some two thousand limestone pillars rising from the Gulf of Tonkin. Its name, the bay of the descending dragon, comes from a legend of dragons spitting jewels to wall off invaders.
Africa's largest lake, known around its shores as Nalubaale and Nyanza. Speke reached it in 1858 and declared it the source of the Nile, a claim argued for twenty years.
The Blue Nile thunders out of Lake Tana into a gorge. The Jesuit Pedro Páez, who saw the source in 1618, was the first European to describe it; Bruce claimed the honour in 1770.
The highest peak in the Alps, long called the Accursed Mountain. Its first ascent, by Balmat and Paccard in 1786, is often taken as the birth of mountaineering.
A volcano on the Armenian highlands where tradition grounded Noah's ark. Friedrich Parrot first climbed it in 1829.
The most honoured of China's five sacred mountains. Emperors climbed it to report to Heaven, the First Emperor among them in 219 BCE.
A granite peak in the south of the Sinai, held to be where Moses received the law. St Catherine's Monastery has stood at its foot since the sixth century.
The world's highest waterfall, falling nearly a kilometre from the flat top of Auyán-tepui. The Pemón call it Kerepakupai Merú; outsiders learned of it from the pilot Jimmie Angel in 1933.
Rome's frontier across northern Britain, eighty Roman miles of stone with a fort every mile. Abandoned when the legions left; Bede described it, and Camden made it famous again in 1586.

The longest waterway people ever dug, carrying the grain of the south to the capitals of the north. It was cut and recut for two thousand years, each age along its own course as the capitals moved; the map follows the route of the age.

phases.name: Early canals
phases.note: The king of Wu cuts the Hangou from the Yangtze to the Huai in 486 BCE; the Honggou soon links the Yellow River to the Huai's tributaries.

phases.name: Sui and Tang
phases.note: Sui joins the old canals into one system in six years: the Tongji from Luoyang to the Huai, the Yongji north to Zhuojun, and the canal south to Hangzhou. Tang feeds its capitals with it.

phases.name: Northern Song
phases.note: The Bian canal brings the grain of the south to Kaifeng, the largest city in the world; the northern branch has silted up.

phases.name: Southern Song
phases.note: The Jin take the north and the Yellow River floods across the Bian; only the canal south of the Yangtze still serves, to the new capital at Hangzhou.

phases.name: Yuan
phases.note: The Mongols cut a straight new course through Shandong to Dadu, the Beijing of today, bypassing Luoyang and Kaifeng; much grain still goes by sea.

phases.name: Ming and Qing
phases.note: Ming reopens the canal in 1411 and from 1604 routes it clear of the Yellow River; for four centuries it carries the grain tribute to Beijing.

phases.name: After 1855
phases.note: The Yellow River swings north and cuts the canal in Shandong; the grain goes by sea and rail, and only the southern reaches stay in use.

story: A great passage tomb older than the pyramids, its passage lit by the rising sun at midwinter. In Irish tradition it was Brú na Bóinne, home of the Dagda; antiquaries found its entrance in 1699.
Some three thousand standing stones in long rows across the Breton heath, raised by the first farmers of the Atlantic coast. Local legend held they were a Roman legion turned to stone.
An abbey on a tidal island, cut off from the land twice a day. Pilgrims crossed the sands to it for centuries; it appears on the Bayeux Tapestry.
A cave painted with horses, aurochs and stags some seventeen thousand years ago. Four teenagers following their dog found it in 1940.
A cave ceiling of bison painted in red and black. A girl looked up and saw them in 1879; for twenty years experts refused to believe anything so fine could be prehistoric.

Hundreds of hands stencilled in red, ochre, black and white on the rock walls above the Pinturas river canyon in Patagonia, among guanacos, rheas and hunting scenes. Hunter-gatherers painted here for some eight thousand years, from about 7300 BCE to 700 CE, blowing pigment around their hands through bone pipes; nearly all the hands are left hands. Alberto De Agostini wrote of it in 1941.
A Buddha seventy-one metres tall carved from the cliff where three rivers meet, to calm the waters for boatmen. It took ninety years to finish.
Two great Buddhas cut into a cliff on the road between India and Central Asia; Xuanzang saw them gilded in 630. They stood fourteen centuries until they were blown up in 2001.

Darius's account of his rise, carved high on a cliff in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Rawlinson copied it hanging from ropes, and it unlocked cuneiform as the Rosetta Stone unlocked hieroglyphs.
A quarter-mile earthwork in the shape of an uncoiling serpent on an Ohio ridge. Who built it, and when, is still argued; Squier and Davis surveyed it in 1846.
The great stupa raised by Ashoka and ringed by carved gateways telling the Buddha's lives. Forgotten as Buddhism faded in India, a British officer recorded it, overgrown, in 1818.
The largest structure made by living things, two thousand kilometres of coral off Queensland. Cook ran aground on it in 1770 and spent weeks repairing the Endeavour.
A pyramid of rock on the Swiss–Italian border. Whymper's party reached its summit in 1865; four of them fell to their deaths on the way down.
The highest mountain outside Asia. Inca priests climbed high on it to make offerings; a Swiss guide first reached the summit in 1897.
The smoking mountain that watches over the Valley of Mexico. Cortés's men climbed it in 1519 to gather sulphur for gunpowder.
An ice-capped volcano long thought the highest mountain on Earth. Humboldt climbed higher on it in 1802 than anyone had been, and drew his famous chart of plants by altitude.
The highest peak in North America, the High One to the Koyukon. Vancouver saw it from the sea in 1794; it was first climbed in 1913.
Geysers, boiling springs and painted canyons over a slumbering supervolcano. John Colter's tales of it in 1807 were laughed at; in 1872 it became the world's first national park.
A river that never reaches the sea, spreading into a vast green delta in the Kalahari. Livingstone crossed its edge on the way to Lake Ngami in 1849.

The largest tropical wetland on Earth, where the upper Paraguay and its rivers flood a basin the size of England each rainy season: caimans, jaguars, capybaras and hyacinth macaws. Spanish explorers going upriver in the 1540s took it for a great lake, the Laguna de los Xarayes, and it sat on European maps as an inland sea for two centuries.
A volcano rising straight from the Gulf of Guinea. The Carthaginian Hanno saw it burning at night around 500 BCE and called it the Chariot of the Gods.
The highest peak of the Southern Alps, Aoraki to the Māori, a boy turned to stone. Tasman saw the great range in 1642; it was named for Cook in 1851.
One of the most active volcanoes on Earth, home of the fire goddess Pele. The missionary William Ellis described its lava lake in 1823.
Granite peaks rising from a sea of cloud, crooked pines on their ledges. Xu Xiake climbed them in 1616 and said that after Huangshan he need see no other mountain.
The highest mountain in Greece, home of the gods in Homer and Hesiod. No one is recorded climbing to its summit until 1913.
A limestone rock guarding the strait between the Mediterranean and the Ocean, one of the Pillars of Hercules. For the ancients it marked the end of the known world.
Some forty thousand basalt columns stepping into the sea, said to be the road of the giant Finn McCool. Reported to the Royal Society in 1693.
The highest great lake in the world, where the Inca said the sun and the first people rose from the water. Cieza de León described it in 1553.
A great shallow lake on the edge of the Sahara, heart of the empire of Kanem-Bornu. Denham, Clapperton and Oudney were the first Europeans to see it, in 1823.
A sandstone plateau of stone forests and painted shelters, its art recording a green Sahara of cattle, giraffes and swimmers. A French officer first reported the paintings in 1933.
The highest volcano in Eurasia, rising over Kamchatka. Cossacks under Atlasov saw it in 1697; Krasheninnikov described it for the Russian Academy.
The hot spring that gave every geyser its name, shooting water high into the Icelandic air. Icelanders recorded its eruptions from 1294.
Norway's longest and deepest fjord, two hundred kilometres into the mountains. Viking fleets sailed from its shores; Romantic painters made it famous in the nineteenth century.
Europe's highest active volcano, the forge of Hephaestus. The philosopher Empedocles was said to have leapt into its crater.
A valley of soft volcanic rock worn into cones and chimneys, carved within into churches and whole underground towns. The traveller Paul Lucas described its strange pinnacles in 1705.
Four hills rising from the Kalahari, painted with thousands of images; to the San, where the first spirit knelt to pray after creating the world.
The southernmost active volcano, smoking over the Ross Sea. James Clark Ross named it for his ship in 1841; Shackleton's men first climbed it in 1908.
Monasteries built on top of sandstone pillars in Thessaly, reached for centuries by ladders and nets hauled up by rope.
Temples of the Chandela kings carved with thousands of figures of gods, dancers and lovers; overgrown when the dynasty fell, they were shown to a British officer in 1838.
A temple to the sun god built as a giant stone chariot with twenty-four carved wheels. Its tower, a landmark for ships in the Bay of Bengal, was known to sailors as the Black Pagoda.
Thirty-four cave temples, Buddhist, Hindu and Jain side by side, among them the Kailasa temple, carved downward from a single mass of rock.
The great crusader castle of the Hospitallers in Syria, which held out for a century and a half until Baybars took it in 1271.
A fortified village of earthen houses on the caravan route from the Sahara to Marrakesh, over the High Atlas.
The walled citadel of the Chachapoya, the Cloud Warriors, on a ridge above the Utcubamba, with walls up to nineteen metres high; forgotten after the Spanish conquest until 1843.
A wall of concrete across the Colorado, built in five years in the Depression, which made Lake Mead and lit the cities of the American South-west.
The largest power station ever built, damming the Yangtze above Yichang; its reservoir drowned towns and temples for six hundred kilometres upstream.
Herod's palace-fortress on a cliff above the Dead Sea, where Jewish rebels held out against Rome until 73 or 74 CE.
One of the first towns, a honeycomb of mud-brick houses entered through the roof, painted with bulls and hunters nine thousand years ago.
The great gilded stupa of Yangon, said to hold eight hairs of the Buddha; the English merchant Ralph Fitch described it in 1586.
The Roman temples of Heliopolis in the Beqaa valley, built on foundation stones weighing up to a thousand tonnes.
A walled hill town with fifty-two towers, besieged in the Albigensian Crusade and rebuilt, rather freely, by Viollet-le-Duc from 1853.
The highest mountain on Earth, Chomolungma to the Tibetans. Measured as Peak XV by the Survey of India in 1852–56 and named for its former head; first climbed in 1953.
Snow-capped mountains on the equator: Ptolemy's Mountains of the Moon, where he placed the source of the Nile. Stanley saw them in 1888.
A broken volcanic peak on the equator, Kirinyaga, the seat of God, to the Kikuyu. The missionary Krapf saw its snows in 1849.
The largest unbroken caldera on Earth, a crater twenty kilometres across full of grazing herds, the land of the Maasai.
The longest freshwater lake in the world, reached by the caravan trade from the Swahili coast at Ujiji; Burton and Speke arrived in 1858.
The highest mountain of Borneo, held by the Kadazan to be the resting place of the dead; Hugh Low climbed it in 1851.
A volcano on Sumbawa whose eruption in 1815, the largest in recorded history, darkened the skies of the world and brought the year without a summer.
A volcano on the border of Korea and Manchuria with a crater lake at its summit, sacred to Koreans and to the Manchu; its eruption around 946 was among the greatest of the last two thousand years.
Once the fourth largest lake in the world, between the deserts of Central Asia. Its rivers were diverted to water cotton from the 1960s, and most of it has dried away.
A volcano that has erupted every few minutes for thousands of years, the lighthouse of the Mediterranean; to the Greeks, the home of Aeolus, keeper of the winds.
A ring of islands around a drowned caldera. Its eruption around 1600 BCE buried the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri under ash.
A marble peak at the end of a peninsula, where Xerxes cut a canal to spare his fleet its storms; a republic of monasteries since the tenth century.
A granite valley in the Sierra Nevada, home of the Ahwahneechee; a militia chasing them entered it in 1851, and in 1864 it was set aside for the public.
The small lake where the Mississippi begins, found in 1832 by Henry Schoolcraft with the Ojibwe guide Ozawindib.
The largest salt flat on Earth, a white plain on the Bolivian altiplano where a prehistoric lake dried away.

A ridge in the Andes south-east of Cusco striped red, gold, turquoise and lavender by its minerals. For as long as anyone remembered it lay under snow and ice; as the ice melted in the early 2010s the colours came out, and photographs of them spread across the world. By 2017 more than a thousand visitors a day were climbing to its 5,200-metre summit.
A fjord between sheer granite walls in the south-west of New Zealand, Piopiotahi to the Māori.

A cliff at the northern end of Europe. The Norse chieftain Ohthere sailed round it about 890 and told King Alfred of the voyage; the English captain Richard Chancellor named it in 1553, looking for a way to China.
The oldest desert on Earth, where red dunes three hundred metres high run down to the Atlantic.
Thousands of sandstone pillars rising from the forest of western Hunan, made a national park in 1982.
Three granite towers at the edge of the Patagonian ice field.

The temple beside the tree under which the Buddha found enlightenment, the goal of pilgrims from China, Korea and Southeast Asia for a thousand years. Faxian and Xuanzang described it; Cunningham surveyed it in 1861 and it was restored in the 1880s.

Built in 652 at Xuanzang's request to keep the scriptures and images he had brought back from India, in the monastery where he spent his last years translating them. It still stands over Xi'an, a little shorter than it was.
The great mud mosque of Timbuktu, built after Mansa Musa came home from his pilgrimage to Mecca, to a design said to be by the Andalusian poet al-Saheli. Caillié saw it in 1828 and Barth in 1853.

The great twin-shrined pyramid of Tenochtitlan, to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc, rebuilt seven times as the city grew. The Spaniards razed it and built Mexico City over it; electricians digging in 1978 struck the great stone of the goddess Coyolxauhqui.

The first great Buddhist monastery in Mongolia, raised by Abtai Khan in 1585 with stones from the ruins of Karakorum, inside a wall crowned by 108 stupas. Most of its temples were destroyed in the purges of 1937; it became a monastery again in 1990.

A bottle-shaped stone tower in the Silla capital, raised under Queen Seondeok to watch the stars: the oldest surviving observatory in East Asia, made of 362 stones, one, it is said, for each day of the lunar year.

An artificial grotto on Mount Toham, built over the eighth century, where a granite Buddha faces the sunrise over the Eastern Sea, surrounded by bodhisattvas and guardians. Restored by the Japanese colonial government from 1913, it is among the masterpieces of Buddhist sculpture.

A trilithon of three coral limestone slabs on Tongatapu, each over five metres tall, raised by the eleventh Tuʻi Tonga around 1200. Its name means 'Maui's burden'; some read the notches on its lintel as marking the solstices.

The fortress-temple above Cusco, its zigzag walls of stones up to a hundred tons fitted without mortar. Manco Inca's army held it during the siege of 1536, and the Spaniards later quarried it to build their city.

The great Hindu temple compound of Java, dedicated to Shiva in 856, its central tower forty-seven metres high. Left as the island's courts moved east and shaken down by earthquakes, it was surveyed in 1811 under British rule.

Rajaraja Chola's temple to Shiva at Thanjavur, completed in 1010, its granite tower sixty-six metres high: the largest temple in India of its day, built by the dynasty whose fleet would strike Srivijaya.

One of the Seven Wonders: a tower perhaps a hundred metres high on the island of Pharos, built under the first Ptolemies, its fire seen far out to sea. Earthquakes brought it down by 1323; Qaitbay built a fort on its stones in 1480, and divers found its blocks on the seabed in 1994.

One of the Seven Wonders: the great marble temple of Ephesus, burned by Herostratus in 356 BCE and rebuilt larger. Destroyed by the end of the fourth century, its site was lost under silt until John Turtle Wood found it in 1869.

One of the Seven Wonders: the tomb of Mausolus, so famous that every great tomb since has been a mausoleum. Earthquakes toppled it, and the Knights of St John used its stones for their castle; Charles Newton found its foundations in 1857.

One of the Seven Wonders: a bronze statue of the sun god Helios over thirty metres tall. It stood for only fifty-four years before an earthquake broke it at the knees; the ruins lay for eight centuries until the bronze was sold for scrap in 654.

One of the Seven Wonders: Phidias's seated Zeus of gold and ivory, twelve metres high, in the temple at Olympia. Carried off to Constantinople, it was lost in a fire; German excavations from 1875 uncovered the temple and, later, Phidias's workshop.
Nebuchadnezzar's gate into Babylon, faced with glazed blue bricks and rows of dragons and bulls. Buried as Babylon emptied, it was dug out by Robert Koldewey from 1902 and rebuilt in a Berlin museum.

The Gothic cathedral on the Île de la Cité, begun in 1163 and finished nearly two centuries later, with its flying buttresses and rose windows. Its spire fell in the fire of 2019 and rose again in 2024.
The basilica raised over the tomb of St Peter, its dome designed by Michelangelo: for centuries the largest church in the world. Envoys from Mexico, Japan and China came to the pope here.
Louis XIV's palace outside Paris, where the court of France lived from 1682 until the Revolution, with its Hall of Mirrors and gardens. The Siamese embassy of 1686 was received here.
Jørn Utzon's shells of white tiles on Bennelong Point, opened in 1973 after sixteen years of building, on a point named for a Wangal man who lived among the first British settlers.
A suspension bridge across the strait into San Francisco Bay, opened in 1937: for nearly thirty years the longest span in the world, painted 'international orange' to stand out in the fog.

The clock tower of the rebuilt Palace of Westminster, finished in 1859 after the old palace burned. Big Ben is properly the great bell inside it, whose chimes the BBC carried around the world from 1923.
The palace-fortress of the Nasrid sultans, the last Muslim rulers of Spain, its courts of water and carved stucco handed over to Ferdinand and Isabella in 1492.
The Flavian amphitheatre, which held some fifty thousand spectators for games and executions. After the last games in 523 it became a quarry, a fortress and finally a monument.
The temple of Athena on the Acropolis. It stood almost whole as a church and then a mosque for two thousand years, until a Venetian shell blew up the powder stored inside in 1687.
Justinian's church of Holy Wisdom, whose dome seemed to hang from heaven; the largest church in the world for a thousand years, a mosque from 1453, a museum from 1934 and a mosque again from 2020.
The golden dome over the rock from which, in Islamic tradition, Muhammad ascended to heaven, on the site of the Jewish Temple; the oldest surviving great Islamic building.
The great mosque of Umayyad Córdoba, a forest of more than eight hundred columns under red and white arches; a cathedral was built in its middle in the sixteenth century.
The fortress of Moscow's princes on a hill above the river, rebuilt in red brick by Italian masters in the 1480s and 1490s, with the cathedrals where the tsars were crowned.
An iron tower three hundred metres high, built for the Exposition of 1889 and meant to stand for twenty years; the tallest structure in the world until 1930.

The largest religious monument in the world, built by Suryavarman II as a temple to Vishnu. When Angkor was abandoned it stayed a Buddhist monastery; a Portuguese friar described it in 1586, and Mouhot's account made it famous in 1860.
The palace of the Ming and Qing emperors, nearly a thousand buildings within purple walls, closed to all but the court; Matteo Ricci entered it in 1601.
Where the emperor prayed each winter for good harvests, its round hall roofed in blue tiles for the sky.
The palace of the Dalai Lamas, rising thirteen storeys up the Red Hill. Two Jesuits sketched it in 1661; photographs reached the world after the British invasion of 1904.
The great temple of Nara, whose Great Buddha Hall, rebuilt in 1709, was long the largest wooden building in the world.
The tomb Shah Jahan built for his wife Mumtaz Mahal in white marble on the Yamuna; the French traveller Bernier described it in 1663.
A copper colossus given by France, holding a torch over New York harbour; for millions of emigrants the first sight of America.
Shah Abbas's great square, half a kilometre long, framed by the royal mosque, the palace and the bazaar; Isfahan, the Persians said, is half the world.
Three madrasas facing one another across Samarkand's central square, the first built by Ulugh Beg, the astronomer prince.

The great shallow lake of the Valley of Mexico, with Tenochtitlan on an island in its western arm, joined to the shore by causeways. Drained from 1607 to stop the city flooding, it was all but gone by 1900.
The salt lake at the end of the Tarim, beside ancient Loulan, which seemed to wander across the desert as the river shifted. Hedin mapped it in 1901; once the Tarim was dammed, it dried up in 1972.

Eleven churches cut down into the solid rock around 1200 for King Lalibela, as a new Jerusalem in the Ethiopian highlands; Bete Giyorgis stands in its pit in the shape of a cross. Francisco Álvares, who saw them in 1521, wrote that he would describe no more for fear of not being believed.
Granite stelae carved as many-storeyed towers, raised over the tombs of Aksum's kings. The greatest, 33 metres long, fell as it was raised; one was taken to Rome in 1937 and returned in 2005.

First built, by tradition, when Djenné's king became Muslim around 1240. The present mosque, raised by the city's masons' guild in 1907, is the largest mud-brick building in the world, replastered by the whole town every spring.
The temple of Amun at Thebes, enlarged by pharaoh after pharaoh for two thousand years into the largest religious complex of the ancient world. Its hypostyle hall holds 134 columns.
Hadrian's temple to all the gods, whose unreinforced concrete dome, open to the sky at its centre, was the largest in the world for 1,300 years. It survived by becoming a church in 609.
A three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge carrying water fifty kilometres to Nîmes, built of stones laid without mortar.
Florence's cathedral, which stood open to the sky for decades because no one knew how to roof it, until Brunelleschi raised the largest brick dome ever built without a wooden frame, finished in 1436.
The bell tower of Pisa's cathedral, which began to lean on its soft ground before the third storey was built. Builders spent two centuries finishing it, curving the upper floors to compensate.
Venice's golden church, built to hold the relics of St Mark smuggled from Alexandria, and later crowned with four bronze horses looted from Constantinople in 1204.
Antoni Gaudí's basilica, begun in 1882 and paid for by donations; he worked on it until his death in 1926, and it is still being finished.
Charlemagne's palace chapel, an octagon modelled on Byzantine churches, where he was buried in 814. German kings were crowned here for six centuries.
A Stone Age village on Orkney, older than the pyramids, with stone beds, dressers and hearths in houses joined by covered passages. A storm stripped the sand from it in 1850.

A fluted tower of red sandstone 73 metres high, begun by the first Delhi sultan as a minaret and victory tower beside a mosque built from the stones of Hindu and Jain temples. An iron pillar of the Gupta age stands in its courtyard.
The holiest shrine of the Sikhs, set in a sacred pool with doors on all four sides, open to all. Ranjit Singh covered its upper storeys in gold around 1830.
The temple of the goddess Meenakshi at the heart of Madurai, rebuilt by the Nayak kings in the 1600s with fourteen gate towers crowded with painted gods.
Akbar's red sandstone capital, where he debated with Muslim, Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian and Jesuit scholars. Abandoned after fourteen years, it stands almost complete.
Cave temples cut into a sandstone cliff by the Northern Wei, with Buddhas up to seventeen metres tall, carved in a style brought along the Silk Road from Gandhara.
More than a hundred thousand Buddhist images carved into the limestone cliffs of the Yi river over four centuries. The great Vairocana Buddha is said to have been given the face of Wu Zetian.

Li Chun's stone bridge over the Xiao river, the oldest standing open-spandrel arch bridge in the world, built some seven centuries before Europe built one. It has carried traffic for fourteen hundred years.
The irrigation works of the Qin governor Li Bing, which split the Min river without a dam to water the Chengdu plain. It still works after more than two thousand years.
A watchtower over the Yangzi, said to be where an immortal flew away on a yellow crane. Cui Hao's and Li Bai's poems made it famous; it burned and was rebuilt many times.
The Qing summer palace beyond the Great Wall, with gardens copying southern China and temples copying Tibet's, including a smaller Potala built to receive Mongol and Tibetan guests.
The fortress at the western end of the Ming Great Wall, the last gate of China for travellers heading west. Bento de Góis waited near here in 1605 for leave to enter.
The Great Mosque of Damascus, built by the caliph al-Walid on the site of a Roman temple and a church, its walls covered in golden mosaics of gardens and cities.

The cube-shaped shrine at the centre of the Great Mosque of Mecca, which Muslims everywhere face in prayer. Ludovico di Varthema, disguised as a Muslim, was the first European known to have seen it, in 1503.
Built by Constantine over the place of Jesus's crucifixion and tomb. Destroyed in 1009 and rebuilt, it is shared today by six Christian churches.
A minaret of carved brick 65 metres tall in a remote Afghan gorge, built by the Ghurid sultans, probably at their lost summer capital of Firozkoh. Outsiders learned of it only in 1957.
The White Heron Castle, the finest surviving castle of Japan's age of wars, with a six-storey keep on a hill. It came through the bombing of 1945 untouched.
A Shinto shrine built over the sea on the holy island of Miyajima by Taira no Kiyomori, whose great red gate seems to float at high tide.

Rice terraces carved up the mountains of northern Luzon by the Ifugao and watered from the forests above. Tradition makes them two thousand years old; radiocarbon dating suggests they spread after the Spanish came.
A concrete and soapstone statue of Christ, thirty metres tall, with arms spread over Rio from the peak of Corcovado.
Four presidents' heads, eighteen metres high, blasted into a granite mountain in the Black Hills, land sacred to the Lakota and taken from them in 1877.
At 828 metres the tallest building in the world since 2010, risen from the desert coast of Dubai.
The walled royal enclosure of Gondar, with castles built by Fasilides and his heirs. James Bruce lived at the court here in 1770.
The volcano over the Bay of Naples, thought extinct until it buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79. Pliny the Younger watched the eruption and described it in two letters.
The second-highest mountain on Earth, in the Karakoram. Thomas Montgomerie of the Survey of India listed it in 1856 as the second peak of the Karakoram range, and the label stuck.
A double-coned extinct volcano, the highest peak of the Caucasus and of Europe. A Kabardian guide, Killar Khashirov, reached its eastern summit in 1829.
The snow-capped volcano above Tehran, the highest peak in the Middle East. In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh the tyrant Zahhak is chained in a cave inside it.
A valley of turquoise lakes and travertine falls named for the nine Tibetan villages along it. Unknown to the rest of China until loggers came in the 1970s; it opened to visitors in 1984.
A waterfall on the Baishui river in Guizhou, falling into a pool with a cave behind its curtain. Xu Xiake described it in 1638.

Where the Yangzi cuts through the Wu mountains in three gorges, the Qutang, Wu and Xiling, whose rapids boatmen hauled through for centuries. Thomas Blakiston sailed up them in 1861. The dam downstream has since raised the water.
White terraces of travertine left by hot springs flowing down a hillside, the Cotton Castle in Turkish. The Greek spa town of Hierapolis was built above them.
A desert valley of red sand and sheer sandstone mountains in southern Jordan, carved with Nabataean inscriptions. T. E. Lawrence rode through it in 1917 during the Arab Revolt.

Volcanic islands on the equator, named for their giant tortoises. Inca tradition tells of Tupac Yupanqui sailing to islands far out to sea, perhaps these; the Bishop of Panama drifted onto them in 1535, and Darwin's visit in 1835 helped lead him to the theory of evolution.
A flat-topped tepui with sheer cliffs on all sides, where Brazil, Venezuela and Guyana meet. First climbed in 1884, it inspired Conan Doyle's The Lost World.
A volcano that rose from a farmer's cornfield in Michoacán in February 1943 and grew to 424 metres over nine years, burying two villages.
An island born from an undersea eruption off Iceland in 1963, named for the fire giant Surtr. Scientists have kept it closed to watch life arrive.
Chalk cliffs facing France across the narrowest part of the Channel. Caesar's fleet found them lined with British warriors in 55 BCE and had to land further along.
The flat-topped mountain above the Cape of Good Hope, Hoerikwaggo, the mountain in the sea, to the Khoekhoe. António de Saldanha climbed it in 1503 and named it.
Five flat-topped peaks in Shanxi held to be the home of the bodhisattva Manjushri, drawing pilgrims from India, Tibet, Korea and Japan. Ennin climbed them in 840.
The rocky headland at the tip of the Cape Peninsula. Dias rounded it in 1488 and, it is said, called it the Cape of Storms; the king renamed it for the hope of India.
The bay where Dias's men first landed in southern Africa in 1488, and da Gama traded with the Khoekhoe in 1497. A tree here was the first post office of the Indian Ocean.
